title: UK Doubles Settlement Wait to Ten Years, Keeps Five-Year Route for Care Workers
excerpt: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's earned-settlement plan doubles the standard ILR wait from five years to ten, applied retrospectively — but care workers earning at least £25,000 who met their visa conditions, higher earners, and many public sector workers keep a five-year route.
body:
• The standard wait for UK settlement (indefinite leave to remain) will double from five years to ten under plans Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood set out in Parliament on Monday, November 2 — and the rules will apply retrospectively to workers already in Britain.
  • Care workers keep a five-year route if they have met their visa conditions and earn at least £25,000 a year; care workers who do not qualify can apply for a new five-year visa and then seek settlement.
  • Earnings decide speed for everyone else: at least £50,271 a year keeps settlement at five years, more than £125,000 brings it down to three, and many skilled public sector workers such as doctors, nurses and teachers also stay at five.
  • The changes are due to take effect next year. GOV.UK's current guidance still sets five years for Skilled Worker and Health and Care Worker settlement — if you are close to qualifying under today's rules, check your position now.

If you are an Indian national working in Britain on a work visa and counting down to permanent residence, the countdown has changed. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood told Parliament on Monday, November 2, that the standard qualifying period for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) — the status that lets a person live and work in Britain permanently and claim some welfare benefits — will double from five years to ten. The change will be applied retrospectively to workers already in Britain, Reuters reported.

Who Is Affected — Exactly

The new default of ten years applies to most legal migrants on work routes who do not fall into a faster category below. Three groups keep a shorter wait. First, care workers: hundreds of thousands in the care sector are exempt from the longer wait and can settle after five years if they have met the conditions of their visas and earn at least £25,000 a year, Reuters reported. Care workers who do not qualify for five-year settlement will be able to apply for a new five-year visa and then seek settlement once that is completed. Second, higher earners: those earning at least £50,271 a year can qualify after five years, and those earning more than £125,000 can qualify in three. Third, many skilled public sector workers — doctors, nurses and teachers among them — will be able to settle after five years.

Everyone seeking settled status will also need a clean criminal record, English spoken to the equivalent of A-level English as a foreign language, no debt owed to the taxpayer, and a record of sustained National Insurance contributions, Mahmood said. Refugees face a separate, much longer track: those who arrived by small boat could wait 20 years, rising to 30 if they do not enter work or study.

"Those who contribute most will settle fastest. Those who don't play by the rules will be refused or wait longer."

— Shabana Mahmood, Home Secretary

Before and After

Until now, legal migrants have generally waited five years before they could be granted ILR. The government's earlier proposal, announced last year, would have required lower-skilled workers to wait 10 to 15 years. The care-worker exemption is a retreat from that proposal, made after a backlash from unions and parts of the governing Labour Party; Housing Secretary Angela Rayner had called retrospective application "un-British." Even with the exemptions, the government said the policy will reduce by 500,000 the number of migrants who arrived since 2021 and would qualify for residence by 2030, while 1.4 million will still qualify in that period. Mahmood told the BBC that around 500,000 people who are due to settle at five years will not now do so.

The mechanism is a shift from time served to contribution: settlement is earned faster by higher earnings, public service work and sustained contributions, and more slowly by those the government says have not played by the rules.

When It Takes Effect, and What To Do Now

The changes are due to take effect next year; the announcement itself does not change anyone's status today. That timing matters. The current rules, as published on GOV.UK's indefinite leave to remain pages, still provide that a person on a Skilled Worker, Health and Care Worker or Tier 2 visa may be able to settle after living and working in the UK for five years, meeting the salary requirements and remaining needed for their job. Under the GOV.UK guidance for those routes, the earliest you can apply is 28 days before you complete five years on a qualifying visa, the fee is £3,226 per person, and GOV.UK warns against waiting until your current visa expires.

So the practical position is this. If you are approaching five years under the current rules, check your eligibility on GOV.UK now and take regulated immigration advice on applying under the rules in force today, because the government has said the new periods will be applied retrospectively once they take effect. If you are a care worker, your five-year route survives only with your visa conditions met and earnings of at least £25,000 — keep the payslips and sponsorship records that prove both. If you earn under £50,271 and are not in an exempt group, plan on the ten-year default and the new contribution tests. Full reporting on the announcement is available from Reuters.
image_caption: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood leaves 10 Downing Street in London. The government plans to double the qualifying wait for permanent settlement to ten years, while care workers keep a five-year route if they meet visa and earnings conditions.
nri_angle: Indians are one of the largest groups on UK work and health and care visas, so the doubled ten-year default — and the care-worker and salary carve-outs — directly change settlement timelines for thousands of Indian families in Britain.
author: Diaspora Desk
